project.title: Your Oppression: Our Aesthetic
project.description: A critical examination of documentary atrocity photography reappropriated as album art in anarcho-punk, hardcore, and powerviolence, ca. 1988–2017.
project.content_warning_global: This project contains historical documentary photographs depicting war crimes, state violence, executions, mass casualties, and human suffering. Images are presented in critical context to examine the ethics of aesthetic reappropriation, not for shock value. All high-sensitivity images are blurred by default and require affirmative user action to view.

curatorial_notes.grouping: Images 5–6 (West Side Horizons), 10–12 (Despise You / ANb split), and 18–19 (Crossed Out 7") are grouped as multi-image records representing a single release.
curatorial_notes.provenance_gaps: Unconfirmed attributions are flagged with 'confidence': 'probable' or 'unconfirmed'. Fields marked 'pending_research' require further archival work.
curatorial_notes.pulitzer_prize_note: Three images in this collection are confirmed Pulitzer Prize-winning photographs used without attribution: Image 7 (Forman, 1977), Image 14 (Faas & Laurent, 1972), Images 18–19 (Razmi, 1980).
curatorial_notes.magnum_note: Three images are confirmed works by Magnum Photos members: Image 8 (George Rodger, co-founder), Image 15 (Gilles Peress), Image 20 (possible Gilles Peress, unconfirmed).

images.album: Deploying All Means Necessary – Issue Two
images.label: Mortarhate Records

source_image.description: Hiroshima 1945 showing the Genbaku Dome after the atomic bomb attack, August 1945.
source_image.photographer: Unknown — stock rights held by Pictorial Press Ltd

alt_text.brief: A lone figure stands amid rubble before the partially standing Hiroshima Genbaku Dome, August 1945.
alt_text.detailed: Black and white photograph of a lone figure, back to camera, standing on a field of debris. The skeletal iron framework of the Hiroshima Genbaku Dome rises against a cloudy sky. Text reads 'Deploying All Means Necessary Issue Two' and 'Conflict'.
alt_text.contextual: The Genbaku Dome is the only structure left standing near the epicenter of the August 1945 atomic bombing of Hiroshima, which killed an estimated 70,000–140,000 people. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The image is commercially licensed through Alamy (Pictorial Press Ltd); its uncredited use constitutes a rights violation in addition to the ethical concerns around decontextualization.

images.historical_context: The United States dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945, killing an estimated 70,000–80,000 people immediately and up to 140,000 by end of 1945. The Genbaku Dome was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.
images.critical_framework: Conflict's use of this photograph follows an anarcho-punk tradition of deploying shocking documentary imagery for anti-war rhetoric. The photograph's familiarity risks domesticating the horror it depicts into album-cover shorthand. The image is commercially licensed; its use without credit is a rights violation.
images.aesthetic_tradition: Anarcho-punk; Crass Records design lineage; anti-nuclear protest imagery
sources: Alamy stock archive — Pictorial Press Ltd
Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum, hiroshimaforpeace.com

images.label: Deep Six Records

source_image.description: Student protester being arrested by Berkeley police, 1964.
source_image.photographer: Unknown — wire service photography, University of California Berkeley Free Speech Movement
source_image.archive: Potential sources: UC Berkeley Bancroft Library; AP Images; Getty Images

alt_text.brief: Black and white photograph of a student protester being arrested by Berkeley police during the 1964 Free Speech Movement.
alt_text.detailed: High-contrast black and white image showing a young person in a white t-shirt being restrained by two uniformed police officers, one pressing a baton across the person's throat from behind.
alt_text.contextual: The Free Speech Movement at UC Berkeley (1964–65) demanded the right to organize politically on campus. The Sproul Hall sit-in of December 2–3, 1964 resulted in approximately 800 arrests — the largest mass arrest in California history at that time. The specific individual depicted is unidentified.

images.historical_context: The FSM is considered a formative event in the 1960s American protest movement. The Berkeley Police Department and Alameda County Sheriff's Department made mass arrests of student protesters during the Sproul Hall sit-in, December 1964.
images.critical_framework: Disrupt were a Boston-based anarcho-crust band active 1989–1995. The Rest (2007) is a posthumous compilation. The FSM context — a nonviolent student protest against institutional censorship — is entirely erased by the image's use as generic signifier of state repression.
images.aesthetic_tradition: Anarcho-crust; anti-police visual rhetoric in DIY hardcore
sources: UC Berkeley Bancroft Library, Free Speech Movement Archives
AP Images historical archive

images.label: Deep Six Records

source_image.description: Viet Cong prisoner with mouth and eyes taped, seated in grass with U.S. soldiers in background.

alt_text.brief: Paul Schutzer photograph, LIFE 1965: a Viet Cong prisoner blindfolded and gagged, kneeling in a rice paddy.
alt_text.detailed: Color photograph of a young man in dark clothing kneeling in tall green rice plants. His eyes and mouth are covered with cloth; a paper processing tag is attached to his chest. LIFE photographer Paul Schutzer, 1965.
alt_text.contextual: Paul Schutzer (1930–1967) was a LIFE magazine staff photographer killed in the Six-Day War in 1967. This 1965 photograph documents the detention of a suspected Viet Cong prisoner with sensory deprivation and a prisoner-processing tag. The practices depicted frequently violated the Geneva Conventions. The image is © Time Inc. Its uncredited use on album art constitutes a rights violation.

images.historical_context: U.S. and ARVN forces detained large numbers of suspected Viet Cong fighters and civilians during the Vietnam War (1955–1975). Interrogation practices frequently violated the Geneva Conventions. Paul Schutzer was embedded with U.S. forces when he took this photograph in 1965.
images.critical_framework: Infest's use of this LIFE magazine photograph without attribution reproduces the colonial gaze of the original documentation. The image is © Time Inc. and its use constitutes both a rights violation and an ethical failure to acknowledge the specific person depicted.
images.aesthetic_tradition: Powerviolence; anti-war visual culture; Deep Six Records aesthetic
sources: LIFE photo archive, TimeLife_image_5906043
Faas, Horst, and Tim Page, eds. Requiem. Random House, 1997.

images.label: Self-released / Gern Blandsten Records

source_image.description: Head of North Korean Soldier.
source_image.archive: Syracuse University Library Special Collections (Margaret Bourke-White Papers); Getty Images/LIFE archive

alt_text.brief: Probable Margaret Bourke-White photograph: a severed or deceased North Korean soldier's head.
alt_text.detailed: Black and white photograph. A uniformed soldier smiles toward the camera at center-left. A disembodied hand enters from the upper right, holding a severed human head by the hair. The head shows signs of trauma.
alt_text.contextual: Margaret Bourke-White (1904–1971) was one of the most significant American photojournalists of the 20th century, documenting WWII, the partition of India, and the Korean War for LIFE magazine. If confirmed, her authorship means this image has a known creator whose estate and archive hold rights. Its use without attribution on a 1991 hardcore split erases a significant photographic legacy.

images.historical_context: Margaret Bourke-White covered the Korean War extensively for LIFE magazine, 1950–53. The Korean War (1950–53) involved extensive atrocities by all parties. Specific event and photograph circumstances unconfirmed pending archive verification.
images.critical_framework: Neanderthal's use of this photograph without any contextual framing renders a specific wartime atrocity as aesthetic provocation, entirely erasing the identity and humanity of the victim.
sources: Syracuse University Library Special Collections, Margaret Bourke-White Papers
Getty Images/LIFE archive

images.label: Pessimiser Records

source_image.description: Mariella, East New York, New York, 1992.
source_image.title: Mariella

alt_text.brief: Eugene Richards photograph, East New York, 1992: extreme close-up of a person holding a syringe at their mouth.
alt_text.detailed: Black and white close-up. A dark-skinned face fills the frame, one eye visible. A hypodermic syringe is held horizontally at the mouth. From Eugene Richards' Cocaine True, Cocaine Blue documentary series, East New York, 1992. Subject named Mariella.
alt_text.contextual: Eugene Richards (born 1944) is an American documentary photographer whose work on poverty and drug addiction in the U.S. involved sustained, long-term community access. Mariella is a named subject photographed in East New York during the crack epidemic. Her appearance on the album cover without credit erases that specificity.

source_image.description: A figure walks through the rubble-filled interior of a destroyed building.

alt_text.brief: A figure walks through the ruins of a bombed or destroyed building.
alt_text.detailed: Black and white photograph. A single figure in dark clothing walks through the gutted interior of a destroyed building. Twisted metal and debris fill the space.
alt_text.contextual: Source photograph unconfirmed. Visual characteristics consistent with mid-20th-century conflict or bombing aftermath photography.

images.historical_context: Despise You formed in Inglewood/West LA in 1994. Eugene Richards' Cocaine True, Cocaine Blue (1994) documented crack cocaine use in East New York, Denver, and North Philadelphia with sustained community access. East New York was among the neighborhoods most severely affected by the crack epidemic and austerity-era collapse of public services.
images.critical_framework: Despise You's visual program draws on conditions proximate to their own community. Eugene Richards is a living photographer with an established documentary practice built on long-term community relationships. Mariella is a named subject; her appearance without credit or consent acknowledgment raises specific ethical concerns distinct from the anonymous archival imagery elsewhere in this collection.
images.aesthetic_tradition: West Coast powerviolence; Pessimiser Records aesthetic; documentary realism
sources: Richards, Eugene. Cocaine True, Cocaine Blue. Aperture, 1994.

images.label: Self-released

source_image.description: The Soiling of Old Glory: Joseph Rakes attacking Ted Landsmark with a flagpole during the Boston anti-busing protests, City Hall Plaza, April 5, 1976.

alt_text.brief: Stanley Forman's Pulitzer Prize-winning photograph, 1977: Joseph Rakes attacking Ted Landsmark with an American flag during the 1976 Boston anti-busing protests.
alt_text.detailed: High-contrast black and white halftone. A white man in dark clothing lunges forward, using a flagpole bearing an American flag as a weapon toward a Black man in a light suit. A crowd fills the background. INFEST logo at bottom.
alt_text.contextual: Stanley Forman's photograph won the 1977 Pulitzer Prize for Spot Photography. Ted Landsmark, the man attacked, is a Black attorney and civic leader who has spoken publicly and extensively about the photograph's impact on his life. Joseph Rakes was a white anti-busing protester. The image documents a specific act of racist violence during the Boston busing crisis (1974–1988). Its use without credit removes it from this specific political history.

content_warnings: use of national symbol as weapon
images.historical_context: The Boston school desegregation and busing crisis (1974–1988) was among the most violent responses to court-ordered school integration in the United States. Ted Landsmark went on to serve as president of the Boston Architectural College.
images.critical_framework: This is one of three confirmed Pulitzer Prize-winning photographs in this collection used without attribution. Landsmark's personhood and ongoing public life make the decontextualization particularly pointed. The image is widely licensed; uncredited use is also a rights violation.
images.aesthetic_tradition: Powerviolence; political hardcore; anti-racist visual rhetoric
sources: Forman, Stanley. The Soiling of Old Glory. Boston Herald American, April 6, 1976.
Pulitzer Prize Board. 1977 Spot News Photography citation.
Formisano, Ronald P. Boston Against Busing. University of North Carolina Press, 1991.

images.label: Slap-a-Ham Records

source_image.description: A young survivor walks along a road lined by the corpses of hundreds of prisoners who died at the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp, May 1945.
source_image.magnum_note: George Rodger was a co-founder of Magnum Photos (1947).

alt_text.brief: George Rodger photograph, Bergen-Belsen, May 1945: a young child survivor walks past hundreds of bodies at the liberated concentration camp.
alt_text.detailed: Black and white photograph. A child approximately 5–8 years old, in a skirt and jacket, walks along a path past bodies lying on the ground. Bare trees line the background. Capitalist Casualties logo overlaid in pink.
alt_text.contextual: George Rodger (1908–1995) was a British photojournalist and co-founder of Magnum Photos. He was among the first photographers to enter Bergen-Belsen following its liberation by British forces on April 15, 1945. Approximately 13,000 bodies lay unburied at liberation. Rodger later said he was disturbed by his own detachment while composing these photographs and subsequently refused to cover war. The image is held and licensed by Getty Images.

images.historical_context: Bergen-Belsen was liberated by British forces on April 15, 1945. Over 60,000 prisoners were held at liberation; approximately 13,000 bodies lay unburied. Bergen-Belsen survivor records are documented by institutions including Yad Vashem and the USHMM.
images.critical_framework: This is one of the most significant photographs in the collection in terms of provenance weight. George Rodger is a Magnum co-founder; the image is actively licensed by Getty Images. Its use as album art without attribution is among the most ethically serious instances in this set.
images.aesthetic_tradition: Powerviolence; DIY hardcore; Slap-a-Ham Records visual culture
sources: Getty Images — Time & Life Pictures / George Rodger
Yad Vashem Photo Archive, yadvashem.org
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, ushmm.org

images.label: Deep Six Records

source_image.description: Probable documentation of racial violence or lynching. Subject possibly identified as Robert McDaniels.
source_image.subject: Robert McDaniels (probable — may be subject name rather than photographer)
source_image.archive_note: The Eraza Collection is an archive of photographs related to racial violence in the United States. Its provenance strongly suggests this image depicts a victim of racial violence or lynching.

alt_text.brief: Probable racial violence or lynching documentation from the Eraza Collection, heavily processed with extreme contrast.
alt_text.detailed: Extreme high-contrast black and white image. A figure's torso and arms are visible; the wrists appear restrained above the head. The heavy graphic processing obscures detail. DISRUPT and DISRUPT DEAD text in rough lettering.
alt_text.contextual: The Eraza Collection archives photographs of racial violence in the United States. If this photograph depicts lynching — as the provenance suggests — it documents a specific act of racist terror against a specific person. The graphic processing that obscures the image does not mitigate this; it renders a specific atrocity into abstract aesthetic texture. Released in 2007, not 1991.

images.historical_context: The Equal Justice Initiative estimates more than 4,000 racial terror lynchings occurred in the American South between 1877 and 1950. Photographs of lynchings were frequently taken as souvenirs. These images have since been archived as historical documentation of racial violence.
images.critical_framework: This is the only image in the collection drawn from the American racial terror archive. That distinction — domestic racial violence versus international conflict — matters significantly for critical framing. The 2007 release date removes any argument from historical context about awareness of these concerns.
sources: Eraza Collection
Without Sanctuary: Lynching Photography in America (archive and exhibition)

images.label: Relapse Records

source_image.description: Street documentary photograph, Los Angeles.

alt_text.brief: Joseph Rodriguez photograph (credited in liner notes): night street scene showing two young men standing while another person is on the ground nearby.
alt_text.detailed: Color photograph, dark and grainy. Two young men in jackets stand on a sidewalk. A third person is visible in the lower right, hunched or collapsed. Despise You and Agoraphobic Nosebleed logos overlaid.
alt_text.contextual: Joseph Rodriguez documented Los Angeles gang life and poverty across multiple decades, producing East Side Stories (1998). His credited involvement here represents a departure from the uncredited appropriation characterizing most releases in this collection.

source_image.description: Two Iraqi girls watch a U.S. soldier on patrol in the Dora neighborhood of Baghdad.
source_image.note: Chris Hondros (1970–2011) was a Getty Images staff photographer killed in Misrata, Libya in April 2011 — the same year this album was released. He was posthumously awarded the Robert Capa Gold Medal.

alt_text.brief: Chris Hondros / Getty Images: two Iraqi girls on a couch watching a U.S. soldier on patrol in Baghdad's Dora neighborhood.
alt_text.detailed: Color photograph across a gatefold. Left panel: two girls approximately 5 and 8 years old on a patterned couch. Right panel: a soldier in desert camouflage with a rifle across their lap. Despise You logo at far left.
alt_text.contextual: Chris Hondros was one of the most significant photojournalists of the Iraq War. He was killed in Libya in April 2011, the same year this album was released. The Dora neighborhood of Baghdad experienced severe sectarian violence during 2006–08. The image is held by Getty Images.

source_image.description: Street documentary photograph, Los Angeles. Liner notes credit Joseph Rodriguez.

alt_text.brief: Probable Joseph Rodriguez photograph: a child lies on a sun-lit sidewalk outside a storefront.
alt_text.detailed: Color photograph. A young child lies on concrete in bright sunlight. A storefront advertising breakfast hours is visible behind. Liner notes text overlaid crediting recording locations and photography.
alt_text.contextual: Liner notes credit 'Cover photo by Joseph Rodriguez.' Rodriguez's documentary work on poverty in Los Angeles gives this image a specific archival context absent from most releases in this collection.

images.historical_context: Agoraphobic Nosebleed formed in 1994 in western Massachusetts. The Iraq War (2003–2011) produced extensive photojournalism documenting civilian life under occupation. Chris Hondros was killed in Libya in April 2011. The release is notable for partially credited documentary photography.
images.critical_framework: This release is the strongest example in the collection of credited documentary photography. The credited Joseph Rodriguez work and the identifiable Hondros photograph mark a clear departure from anonymous reappropriation. However, consent of photographic subjects — particularly the children in Image 11 — remains unaddressed.
images.aesthetic_tradition: Powerviolence; documentary realism; Relapse Records production aesthetic
sources: Rodriguez, Joseph. East Side Stories: Gang Life in L.A. powerHouse Books, 1998.
Getty Images — Chris Hondros archive
Relapse Records release documentation, 2011.

images.label: Desperate Attempt Records

source_image.description: U.S. and allied forces conducting interrogation operations on captured Viet Cong personnel, 1967.

alt_text.brief: Heavily processed photograph of Vietnam War prisoner interrogation, 1967, from the PJF Military Collection.
alt_text.detailed: Black and white image with extreme halftone processing. Fragmented forms are assembled in a collage treatment. DROPDEAD logo stenciled in upper left. Source: Vietnam War interrogation operations, 1967, PJF Military Collection.
alt_text.contextual: U.S. and ARVN interrogation operations during the Vietnam War frequently violated the Geneva Conventions. The Phoenix Program (1965–1972), a CIA-directed counter-insurgency operation, was responsible for the capture, torture, and killing of tens of thousands of suspected Viet Cong. The heavy processing applied here simultaneously aestheticizes and erases the specific documented violence.

images.historical_context: The Phoenix Program (1965–1972) resulted in the capture, torture, and killing of an estimated 20,000–40,000 suspected Viet Cong. Interrogation photography from this period was produced as operational documentation and by embedded photojournalists.
images.critical_framework: The extreme graphic processing represents a common DIY aesthetic move in 1990s hardcore — processing source material to near-abstraction. This amplifies visceral impact while erasing the provenance and specificity of the documented violence.
images.aesthetic_tradition: Anarcho-hardcore; situationist collage; photocopied zine aesthetics
sources: PJF Military Collection

images.label: Theologian Records

source_image.description: In newly independent Bangladesh, guerrillas in Dacca use bayonets on December 18, 1971 to torture and kill four men suspected of collaborating with Pakistani militiamen.
source_image.award: Pulitzer Prize for Spot News Photography, 1972
source_image.note: Michel Laurent (1945–1975) was killed covering the fall of Saigon. Horst Faas (1933–2012) won two Pulitzer Prizes.

alt_text.brief: Horst Faas and Michel Laurent / AP, Pulitzer Prize 1972: Mukti Bahini guerrillas executing suspected Pakistani collaborators in Dacca, December 18, 1971.
alt_text.detailed: Black and white photograph. A uniformed figure stands over a man lying face-down on grass, striking him with a rifle or club. A crowd of soldiers and civilians forms a circle. INFEST logo with double underline in lower left.
alt_text.contextual: This AP photograph by Horst Faas and Michel Laurent won the 1972 Pulitzer Prize for Spot News Photography. It documents the execution of suspected Pakistani collaborators in Dacca two days after Bangladeshi independence, December 18, 1971. Michel Laurent was killed in 1975; Horst Faas won a second Pulitzer in 1965. The Associated Press holds the rights.

images.historical_context: The Bangladesh Liberation War (1971) followed Operation Searchlight, a genocidal campaign killing an estimated 300,000 to 3,000,000 people. Bangladesh declared independence March 26, 1971; Pakistan surrendered December 16, 1971. The photograph was taken two days after independence during retributive violence against suspected collaborators.
images.critical_framework: This is one of three confirmed Pulitzer Prize-winning photographs in this collection. The Associated Press holds the rights. The use of this photograph collapses the specific political history of Bangladeshi independence — genocide, liberation war, retributive violence — into generic album-cover imagery.
sources: Associated Press archive
Pulitzer Prize Board. 1972 Spot News Photography citation.
Bass, Gary J. The Blood Telegram. Knopf, 2013.

images.label: Deep Six Records

source_image.description: Srebrenica genocide mass grave at Pilica farm, excavated by forensic pathologists in 1996. Twenty feet deep and a hundred feet long.
source_image.publication: The Graves: Srebrenica and Vukovar (Scalo Books, 1998)
source_image.casualty_note: At least 8,372 men, children, and elderly were summarily executed and dumped into mass graves during the 1995 Srebrenica genocide.

alt_text.brief: Gilles Peress / Magnum Photos: Srebrenica genocide mass grave at Pilica farm, 1996. At least 8,372 people were executed and buried here in 1995.
alt_text.detailed: Black and white photograph. The entire frame is filled with decomposed human remains in a mass grave. INFEST logo in lower right corner. Photograph by Gilles Peress from The Graves: Srebrenica and Vukovar (Scalo Books, 1998).
alt_text.contextual: Gilles Peress (born 1946) is a French-American documentary photographer and Magnum Photos member. His book The Graves is a major work of documentary testimony to the Srebrenica genocide. The ICTY and ICJ ruled the 1995 killings a genocide. Forensic excavations identified victims through DNA analysis. The image is © Gilles Peress / Magnum Photos. Its use without attribution in 2013 — 18 years after the genocide — collapses a specific, documented, legally adjudicated atrocity into album-cover imagery.

images.historical_context: The Srebrenica massacre (July 1995): Bosnian Serb forces under General Ratko Mladić systematically murdered at least 8,372 Bosniak Muslim men and boys. The ICTY and ICJ ruled the killings a genocide. Forensic excavations began in 1996; DNA identification work continued for years.
images.critical_framework: This is the most recently documented atrocity in the collection. Gilles Peress is a living photographer; Magnum Photos actively licenses his work. By 2013, the Srebrenica genocide was extensively documented in the public record. The complete absence of contextual framing makes the photograph function purely as aesthetic provocation.
images.aesthetic_tradition: Powerviolence; shock aesthetics in DIY hardcore
sources: Peress, Gilles. The Graves: Srebrenica and Vukovar. Scalo Books, 1998.
Magnum Photos — Gilles Peress archive
International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia (ICTY)

images.label: Deep Six Records

source_image.description: Aerial press photograph of a car crash scene on a city street, with a body covered by a sheet on the sidewalk.
source_image.archive: International Center of Photography (ICP) Weegee archive; Getty Images Weegee/ICP collection

alt_text.brief: Aerial press photograph, probable Weegee, New York City: a car crash scene with a covered body on the sidewalk.
alt_text.detailed: Black and white photograph taken from above. A damaged black automobile on a city street corner, surrounded by onlookers. A body covered by a white sheet lies on the sidewalk to the lower right.
alt_text.contextual: Probable attribution to Weegee (Arthur Fellig, 1899–1968), New York City press photographer who monitored police radio and covered crime and accident scenes. His work appeared in tabloid newspapers and was later recognized as significant art photography. The ICP holds the primary Weegee archive. Attribution pending archive verification.

images.historical_context: Weegee operated primarily in New York City from the late 1930s through the 1940s, covering crime scenes, accidents, and fires. His book Naked City was published in 1945. His subjects were overwhelmingly working-class and immigrant New Yorkers.
images.critical_framework: If confirmed as Weegee, this photograph has a known creator and an institutional rights holder (ICP). Its use without credit is a rights issue in addition to the ethical concerns about humanizing photographic subjects.
sources: International Center of Photography, Weegee Archive, icp.org
Getty Images Weegee/ICP collection

images.label: React! Records

source_image.description: Romania — Interior of the plant for 'incurably ill,' 1990.

alt_text.brief: James Nachtwey photograph, Romania 1990: a person in an institution for the 'incurably ill' sits hunched on a dismantled bed frame in a bare room.
alt_text.detailed: Black and white photograph. A person sits or crouches on a stripped metal bed frame, head lowered toward their knees. The room is bare and deteriorated. James Nachtwey, Romania, 1990. Image code DG-1763.
alt_text.contextual: James Nachtwey (born 1948) is an American documentary photographer widely considered one of the most significant war photographers of the 20th century. His 1990 work in Romania documented catastrophic conditions in post-Ceaușescu institutions for people with disabilities, labeled 'incurably ill' — many of whom were healthy children abandoned due to poverty under the regime's economic policies. Nachtwey is a living photographer whose work is actively licensed. The image was used without attribution or credit in 2017.

images.historical_context: Following the fall of Ceaușescu in December 1989, photographers entering Romania documented catastrophic conditions in state institutions. Nachtwey's photographs contributed to international pressure for reform. The conditions were a direct consequence of Ceaușescu's pronatalist policies combined with economic collapse.
images.critical_framework: James Nachtwey is a living photographer. This is the most temporally recent uncredited appropriation in the collection — 27 years after the photograph was taken. Despise You have no documented connection to Romania or its institutional history. The subject's vulnerability — institutionalized, unclothed, isolated — raises specific ethical concerns about the conditions of the photograph's making and its subsequent use as album art.
sources: Nachtwey, James. DG-1763. 1990.

images.label: Slap-a-Ham Records

source_image.description: Eleven alleged enemies of the Iranian revolution are executed in Sanandaj, Iran, August 27, 1979.
source_image.agency: Ettela'at newspaper, Tehran / distributed by UPI
source_image.award: Pulitzer Prize for Spot News Photography, 1980 — awarded anonymously; Razmi confirmed December 5, 2006
source_image.camera: Nikon FE, Nikkor 28mm lens, Kodak ASA 400 Tri-X film

alt_text.brief: Jahangir Razmi / UPI, Pulitzer Prize 1980: eleven people executed by firing squad in Sanandaj, Iran, August 27, 1979.
alt_text.detailed: Black and white halftone. Armed figures crouch and aim rifles in the foreground. Blindfolded figures in civilian clothing stand or kneel in the middle distance. Arid landscape behind. Crossed Out logo lower right.
alt_text.contextual: Jahangir Razmi's photograph won the 1980 Pulitzer Prize for Spot News Photography — the only anonymous Pulitzer in the award's history at that time, withheld for Razmi's safety. His authorship was confirmed publicly in 2006. The photograph documents the execution of eleven people identified as enemies of the Islamic Revolution in Sanandaj, Kurdistan Province, August 27, 1979. Razmi lives in Tehran.

source_image.description: Wider frame of the same execution in Sanandaj, Iran, August 27, 1979. Same series as cover image.

alt_text.brief: Jahangir Razmi / UPI, Pulitzer Prize 1980: wider frame of the Sanandaj execution, August 27, 1979, showing more participants and landscape.
alt_text.detailed: Black and white photograph, wider frame than the cover. Armed figures in foreground; blindfolded prisoners in middle distance. Arid landscape, military vehicle partially visible. More participants visible than in cover image.
alt_text.contextual: Same documentary series as the cover image. The two images together suggest deliberate selection from Razmi's coverage of the execution.

images.historical_context: Following the 1979 Islamic Revolution, the Islamic Republic of Iran executed mass numbers of political opponents. A particularly large wave of killings occurred in 1988. Razmi photographed the August 27, 1979 executions in Sanandaj for Ettela'at; UPI distributed the images internationally. The Pulitzer was awarded anonymously due to concerns for Razmi's safety.
images.critical_framework: This is one of three confirmed Pulitzer Prize-winning photographs in this collection. The two images together — both from Razmi's coverage — suggest deliberate selection from a documentary series. Their use collapses the political specificity of post-revolutionary Iran into generic anti-state imagery.
images.aesthetic_tradition: Powerviolence; Slap-a-Ham Records visual culture; anti-state visual rhetoric
sources: Pulitzer Prize Board. 1980 Spot News Photography citation.
UPI archive
Abrahamian, Ervand. Tortured Confessions. University of California Press, 1999.

source_image.description: Armed figures in a residential doorway, person kneeling under duress. Bluebell Hill Terrace, Derry, Northern Ireland. Probable IRA, 1970s–early 1980s.
source_image.location_confirmed: Bluebell Hill Terrace, Derry (Londonderry), Northern Ireland — confirmed by visible street sign
source_image.source_of_identification: Community identification via Reddit; corroborated by street sign. Bluebell Hill Terrace is in Derry.
source_image.archive: Potential: Pacemaker Press International; Museum of Free Derry; Linen Hall Library Political Collection, Belfast
source_image.confidence: probable — location confirmed; photographer and specific event unconfirmed
source_image.correction_note: Previous version incorrectly identified location as Belfast. Bluebell Hill Terrace is in Derry (Londonderry), not Belfast.

alt_text.brief: Red-tinted photograph, Bluebell Hill Terrace, Derry, Northern Ireland: armed figures in a doorway and a person kneeling, probable IRA, circa 1970s–early 1980s.
alt_text.detailed: Monochrome photograph with heavy red tone overlay and grain amplification. A street sign reading 'Bluebell Hill Terrace' is visible upper left. In a doorway at center, a figure holds a weapon. Several other figures are visible including one kneeling on the ground.
alt_text.contextual: Bluebell Hill Terrace is a residential street in Derry. Derry was the site of Bloody Sunday (January 30, 1972) and a primary center of republican resistance throughout the Troubles. The scene is consistent with IRA paramilitary activity in a Catholic residential area. Crossed Out and Man Is the Bastard were both San Jose, California bands with no documented connection to Northern Ireland.

images.historical_context: The Troubles (c. 1968–1998) resulted in over 3,500 deaths. Derry's Bogside neighborhood was the site of the Battle of the Bogside (1969) and Bloody Sunday (1972). The Museum of Free Derry and the Linen Hall Library hold extensive archives of Troubles-era documentation.
images.critical_framework: The visible street sign grounds this image in a specific named place — an unusual degree of geographic specificity. For residents of Bluebell Hill Terrace, the use of their street as a San Jose hardcore album cover is a pointed act of reappropriation. The community's distance from the bands using this image is total.
